slides.label: 3-Forms
slides.notes: Open by changing the unit of measurement. A 1-form measures directed motion and a 2-form measures oriented area. Chapter 35 asks for the next meter: a 3-form reads three tangent directions at once and returns signed volume. The route is determinant first, then wedge-product ledgers, coordinate pullbacks, basis counts, graded signs, and finally integration density.

slides.label: Alternation Locks The Dimension
slides.notes: Make the zero result feel inevitable. Alternation says a slot swap changes the sign. If the two slots contain the same vector, the input did not actually change, so the value must equal its own negative. That is why repeated directions collapse a 3-form measurement, and why a nonzero 3-form cannot live on a two-dimensional tangent space.

slides.label: The Coordinate Volume Form
slides.notes: Use the volume box as the main mental model. The coordinate form dx wedge dy wedge dz evaluates three input vectors by placing them as columns in a determinant. The absolute value is the parallelepiped volume and the sign records orientation. Swapping two columns keeps the same geometric box but reverses the orientation reading.

slides.label: The Wedge Product Is A Determinant Ledger
slides.notes: This slide connects the algebraic expansion to the determinant picture. Three one-forms wedged together produce the signed six-term determinant. Building the same object as a two-form wedged with a one-form compresses the bookkeeping into three cyclic terms. The notebook checks that both ledgers give the same number for the same three edge vectors.

slides.label: Calibrating The Volume Meter
slides.notes: Treat the 3-form as an instrument with calibration tests. A slot swap should flip the sign. A repeated slot should read zero. A linear coordinate change should scale the reading by the determinant of the linear map. These are not separate facts; they are the operational tests for an oriented volume meter.

slides.label: Pullback Creates The Integration Density
slides.notes: Now make coordinate change visible. Pulling back dx wedge dy wedge dz through spherical coordinates means measuring the small coordinate box in ordinary Euclidean volume. The three local edge lengths are dr, r dphi, and r sin phi dtheta, so the volume density is r squared sin phi. The symbolic Jacobian and the geometric edge picture agree.

slides.label: Basis 3-Forms Count Distinct Triples
slides.notes: A basis 3-form needs three distinct coordinate labels. In R2 there are no choices, in R3 there is the single top form, and in R4 there are four independent choices. This is the binomial coefficient C(n,3) appearing as a geometric availability statement rather than a memorized counting formula.

slides.label: Graded Signs Explain Self-Wedges
slides.notes: Use the sign grid as a compact proof. Moving a p-form past a q-form requires p times q one-form swaps, so the sign is minus one to the p q. A 2-form commutes with a 1-form because the sign is positive. Odd-degree forms wedge with themselves to zero by the same sign logic, while an even 2-form can have a nonzero square.

slides.label: From Volume Meters To Integrals
slides.notes: Close by returning to integration. A 3-form field assigns a volume meter at every point. Integrating over an oriented region means sampling small oriented boxes, evaluating the local 3-form on their edge directions, and adding the scalar readings. Orientation, determinant behavior, and density are therefore the same idea at local, algebraic, and integral scales.
